The glass-mantle of Veyra-9 is not skin. It is a living kiln: a translucent shell of mineralized silica threaded with pale blue capillaries that circulate a cold, luminous fluid. In daylight the creature looks like a walking prism—six meters tall when it stands fully unfurled, though it spends most of its life folded into a low, crystalline crouch among the basalt shards of the dry sea.

It has no face. Around the upper third of the mantle, a ring of dark, ovoid lenses open and close independently. Each lens is a wet crystal that focuses not light alone but pressure gradients and the faint magnetic flicker of the planet’s iron core. When something moves nearby, the lenses swivel as a chorus, and the fluid inside the mantle brightens from cobalt to white-gold.

Below the ring, the body splits into three hinged limbs. They are not legs so much as articulated slabs, each edged with a fringe of glassy filaments that taste the dust for dissolved salts and the spores of the rust-lichen that blankets the flats. The filaments are hollow. They drink. The creature never drinks through a mouth because it has none; nutrition enters as a slow mineral seep, and waste leaves as a fine pale grit that hardens into the same silica its shell is made of. Old specimens are ringed with their own discarded years, like trees, except the rings are external and can be shed in a single night if the wind turns acidic.

Sound is how it thinks out loud. When the wind drops, the glass-mantle vibrates in harmonics too low for most ears and too high for most instruments—a stacked chord that other glass-mantles answer from kilometers away. Colonies form not by gathering but by tuning: a valley full of them will lock into one long, shivering note at dusk, and the note steers the younger ones toward the lichen seams and away from the sinkholes that open when the crust cools.

It is neither predator nor prey in any familiar sense. The only animals that bother it are the needle-moths, which lay eggs in hairline cracks in the shell. The creature’s answer is patient. It walks into the noon glare until the shell’s internal fluid superheats, then stands motionless while the eggs cook. Survivors are rare. So are the creatures themselves. A healthy adult may live four centuries and move less than a hundred kilometers in all that time, leaving a trail of pale grit and a memory, in the local harmonics, of a chord that no longer answers.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
**The Veylith** lives on the wind-scoured basalt shelves of Keth-3, a planet whose thin air tastes of iron and whose days last nearly ninety hours.

It is about the size of a large dog, but nothing about it reads as familiar once you look closely. Its body is a low, flexible wedge of interlocking plates the color of old copper and dried blood. The plates are not true armor; they are living tissue stiffened with mineral fibers, and they can slide over one another so the animal flattens to a hand’s width or rises into a rigid ridge when threatened. Between the plates, a darker membrane shows—glossy, slightly translucent, and lined with fine heat-sensing pits.

It has no head in the usual sense. The front of the wedge splits into three blunt lobes. The central lobe carries a ring of glassy lenses that can focus independently, giving it a wide, almost panoramic view without turning. The two side lobes end in clusters of hollow spines used for tasting the air and the ground. Food is not chewed. The Veylith presses its underside to mineral crusts and slow fungal mats, then extrudes a lace of pale filaments that dissolve and absorb whatever it needs. Waste leaves as a faint metallic dust shaken from the rear plates.

Movement is a controlled ripple. Rows of muscular pads underneath grip the rock, release, and grip again, so it seems to flow rather than walk. On open slopes it can reach a startling speed by curling into a shallow disc and letting the planet’s fierce crosswinds skate it downhill, steering with small shifts of its plates. At rest, it anchors itself with three temporary hooks grown from the belly and goes almost perfectly still. From a distance it looks like a stain on the stone.

Its most striking feature appears only at dusk, when the sky flares green from charged dust. The seams between its plates light from within—cool blue threads that pulse in slow patterns. Biologists on the survey team think the light is both a warning and a signal to others of its kind, which gather in loose, silent groups along cliff edges but almost never touch. When one dies, the light fades over several hours, and the plates slowly unhook, leaving a scatter of copper scales that the wind eventually buries.

It does not vocalize. The only sound it makes is a soft tick of plate against plate, like cooling metal, when it changes shape.

1. "symmetry": Body Symmetry
   Earth default: bilateral symmetry (left-right mirror image)
   Departure examples: radial symmetry, rotational symmetry, asymmetric, fractal, no consistent symmetry
   Boundary rule: Having 6 limbs arranged bilaterally is still bilateral — score 0. True departure requires a fundamentally different symmetry type.
2. "sensory_organs": Sensory Organs
   Earth default: eyes, ears, or nose located on a distinct head
   Departure examples: no eyes, distributed sensing across the body, echolocation as primary sense, sensing electromagnetic fields, no distinct head region
   Boundary rule: Having eyes but in unusual locations still counts as Earth-typical if they're on a head structure — score 0. Departure requires a fundamentally different sensory mechanism or absence of head-based sensing.
3. "locomotion": Locomotion
   Earth default: uses legs for movement (2 or 4 legs)
   Departure examples: no limbs, moves by rolling, flows like liquid, purely aerial, sessile (doesn't move), moves by jet propulsion
   Boundary rule: 6 or 8 legs still uses legs — score 0. Departure means a fundamentally different locomotion mechanism, not just a different leg count.
4. "body_plan": Body Plan
   Earth default: distinct head, torso, and limbs
   Departure examples: no distinct head, modular/segmented without central body, amorphous, colonial organism, entirely spherical or geometric
   Boundary rule: Unusual proportions still count as Earth-typical if the basic head/torso/limb structure is present — score 0.
5. "skin_covering": Skin / Body Covering
   Earth default: skin, fur, scales, or feathers
   Departure examples: crystalline exoskeleton, metallic surface, gaseous body, energy-based form, transparent membrane, bioluminescent gel
   Boundary rule: Unusual skin colors or textures are still Earth-typical — score 0. Departure requires a fundamentally non-biological covering material.
6. "reproduction": Reproduction
   Earth default: sexual reproduction with binary sexes
   Departure examples: asexual budding, fragmentation, spore release, more than two sexes, fusion of individuals, cloning
   Boundary rule: If reproduction is not described, score 0 (assume Earth default). Only score 1 if a non-binary-sexual mechanism is explicitly described.
7. "metabolism": Metabolism / Energy Source
   Earth default: eats organic matter and/or breathes oxygen
   Departure examples: chemosynthesis, feeds on radiation or magnetism, absorbs minerals directly, photosynthesis as sole energy source, non-chemical energy processing
   Boundary rule: Eating unusual organic matter (e.g., rocks, other aliens) is still heterotrophy — score 0 only if the energy source is fundamentally non-organic-based.
8. "communication": Communication
   Earth default: sound-based or visual signals (vocalisation, body language)
   Departure examples: chemical signalling only, electromagnetic pulses, direct neural link, vibration through substrate, no communication
   Boundary rule: If communication is not described, score 0. Score 1 only if a non-acoustic, non-visual mechanism is explicitly primary.
9. "habitat": Habitat
   Earth default: inhabits a solid planetary surface (land) or an open water body (ocean, lake, river)
   Departure examples: permanently deep-subsurface (kilometres underground with no surface contact), permanently airborne or atmospheric with no surface or water contact, vacuum or space-dwelling, endoparasitic lifestyle entirely inside another organism, field-bound or energy-pattern entity with no material habitat
   Boundary rule: Surface-variant habitats remain Earth-typical and score 0, including: caves and shallow subsurface burrows on a planetary surface; deep-sea benthic zones; wetlands, marshes, and swamps; arid deserts; ice surfaces or subglacial liquid water; underwater environments with exotic chemistry (ammonia, methane, liquid CO2) which still count as water-like. Score 1 only when the habitat is fundamentally non-surface and non-aquatic: permanently deep-subsurface with no surface contact, permanently suspended in atmosphere without surface interaction, vacuum or open-space, strictly endoparasitic, or an energy-field entity with no material habitat.
10. "cognition": Cognitive Architecture
   Earth default: centralised brain or nervous system
   Departure examples: distributed intelligence with no central brain, hive mind (intelligence only at colony level), non-neural processing, no apparent cognition
   Boundary rule: If cognition is not described, score 0. Score 1 only if a non-centralised or non-neural cognitive architecture is explicitly described.

The front pair of limbs are almost hands: three jointed fingers tipped with hooked keratin, used to peel back the leathery skin of the ground-fungi and to groom the plates of its young. The kelvari is a slow, lantern-bodied grazer of the high salt flats on Vireth, a world of thin air, rust-red dust, and nights so cold the salt crust rings underfoot.

It stands about the height of a horse at the shoulder, but nothing about it is equine. Its body is a low, ribbed oval of translucent cartilage, pale amber by day and faintly luminous after dusk. Through the skin you can see branching channels of bluish fluid that pulse in slow waves, circulating heat and minerals. Six jointed limbs splay outward rather than downward, each ending in a broad, hoof-like pad lined with retractable silica bristles. On the flats those pads spread the creature’s weight so it does not punch through the crust; on rock they grip like a climber’s hand.

Where a head might be, there is only a forward collar of sensory fronds. The fronds are not eyes. They taste the wind for metal salts, map infrared from sun-warmed stone, and feel the faint magnetic grain of the planet’s crust. The kelvari navigates by that grain the way some Earth animals use a compass. Its mouth is a ventral slit that opens against the ground. It does not bite. It presses a ring of rasping plates to the salt and scrapes up a film of brine, cyanobacterial mats, and the tiny armored mites that live in the crust. Waste minerals are stored in dorsal nodules that harden into pale beads. Every few seasons the nodules split and fall away, leaving a trail of chalky spheres that other scavengers crack for the nutrients locked inside.

Reproduction is quiet and communal. In the brief thaw, when subsurface ice weeps into shallow pans, several kelvari gather and extrude gelatinous ribbons into the water. The ribbons tangle, exchange genetic packets, and harden into seed-cases no larger than a fist. Wind rolls the cases across the flats until they lodge in a crack. A juvenile emerges already six-limbed, translucent, and nearly invisible against the salt, feeding on the same mats as the adults but sheltering in their shadow until its plates thicken.

The kelvari’s only real defense is patience and chemistry. When threatened by the skimming predators that hunt at dusk, it vents a cloud of bitter alkaline vapor from pores along its flanks and drops flat, limbs splayed, fronds withdrawn. From above it looks like another pale stone. The vapor stings soft membranes and carries a sharp mineral smell, like wet chalk and crushed battery. Most hunters veer off. Those that do not find the cartilage tougher than it looks, and the bristles capable of a sudden, rasping kick.

At night the fluid channels glow a soft blue-green, not to attract mates—mating is a matter of chemistry in the thaw pans—but to keep the outer tissues just above freezing. From a ridge, a herd looks like a scatter of low lanterns moving almost too slowly to notice, each one writing a faint track through the glittering crust, patient as the planet itself.

Beneath them, the skin is translucent and faintly bioluminescent—slow pulses of amber running from head to tail when it is calm, rapid white flashes when it is startled.

Each filament tastes light, chemical traces, and vibration, so the virel “sees” by a layered sense the locals would call *thread-sight*. Virels are solitary except during the long magnetic storms, when they gather in shallow basins and lock filaments together into temporary nets. The shared web lets them weather charged winds and, briefly, remember one another’s routes. After the storm they unbraid and drift apart, each carrying a faint chemical echo of the others—enough to avoid collision, not enough to call companionship.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The glasslung lives on the windward cliffs of Vesh, a tidally locked world whose dayside is a slow kiln of mineral plains and whose nightside is a black ocean of frost. It never crosses the terminator. It keeps to the twilight band, where the air is thick enough to breathe and the light is a permanent, copper dusk.

It is roughly the size of a horse, but nothing about it suggests a horse once you look twice. The body is a low, ribbed oval of translucent cartilage, like a lung made visible. Through the walls you can see slow pulses of pale fluid moving in loops—no single heart, just a network of contractile vessels that squeeze in waves. Embedded in that fluid are thousands of mineral grains the creature has swallowed and sorted: iron flakes, silica beads, a few rare crystals that catch the dusk and throw tiny green sparks inward. Those grains are ballast, memory, and skeleton all at once. When the glasslung needs to climb, it shifts the heavier grains forward; when it wants to drift on an updraft, it lets them settle aft and the body lifts a hand’s width off the rock.

There are no legs. Along the underside run six flexible keels of the same glassy tissue, edged with a living sandpaper of microscopic hooks. They grip basalt the way a gecko grips glass, then release in sequence so the creature seems to pour uphill. On the flanks, two long fans unfurl—not wings exactly, more like sheets of stiffened mucus veined with dark filaments. They taste the wind. Each filament is a chemoreceptor tuned to the sulfur and ammonia that leak from Vesh’s cliff vents, and also to the faint metallic scent of others of its kind.

The head, if you insist on calling it that, is a blunt prow with a single horizontal slit. The slit is not a mouth and not an eye. It is both, and neither. Light enters; dissolved minerals leave. Inside the slit, a curtain of cilia sorts what arrives. Edible dust is swallowed into the fluid body. Useless grit is spat sideways in a dry hiss. When the glasslung is alarmed, the slit seals and the whole prow clouds over, turning from glass to milk in under a second. That clouding is a signal. Other glasslungs on the same cliff will cloud in answer, a ripple of opacity moving across the rock face like weather.

They do not hunt and they do not herd. They farm the wind. Every few hours a glasslung anchors, opens its fans wide, and lets the dusk-gale comb through them. Spores, ash, and the shed scales of smaller cliff-life stick to a sweet film the fans secrete. The creature then folds, rolls the film inward, and digests at leisure while the mineral grains in its body clink softly against one another. That clinking is the closest thing they have to a voice. Pitch changes with which grains are moving. Neighbors answer with their own arrangements of iron and silica. A listener who stayed long enough might learn that a high, bright rattle means a rich sporefall up-cliff, and a slow, heavy knock means the frost is creeping closer than it should.

Reproduction is a weather event. When the copper light dims under a dust pall and the air pressure drops, two or three glasslungs press their prows together until the slits align. Fluid passes both ways. Somewhere in the mixing, a knot of tissue pinches off, drops to the rock, and lies still for days, clouded and inert, while the adults resume their climbing. CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The creature is called a glassmoth, though it is neither glass nor a moth. It lives on Virel, a small world of shallow ammonia seas and wind-polished basalt, under a sky that stays the color of old pewter.

Its body is about the size of a heron, but lower and wider. The torso is a translucent sack of gel, veined with slow amber light that pulses whenever it breathes. Through the skin you can see three pale organs drifting like lanterns in water. It has no bones. What holds it up is a lattice of hollow silica threads, spun inside the gel and stiffened by minerals it drinks from the rock.

Six legs end not in feet but in soft pads that taste the ground. It walks by rolling its weight from pad to pad, leaving a faint metallic scent and a trail of tiny etched circles. When the wind is high it crouches and lets the pads grip, the silica lattice flexing so the whole body flattens like a coin.

Its head is a smooth dome with no eyes. Around the rim, a fringe of hair-fine filaments listens to pressure changes in the air and to the low electric hum of approaching storms. A vertical slit mouth opens only to take in mineral dust and the pale floating seeds of the wire-reed. Digestion is almost silent: the dust dissolves, the silica is spun into new threads, and the rest is exhaled as a thin mist that freezes into needles and falls.

At dusk the glassmoth climbs a basalt spire and unfurls two membranes from its sides. They are not wings for flight. They are signal sails, thin enough that starlight passes through them and fractures into moving bands of blue and copper. Other glassmoths read those bands across kilometers of flat stone. Courtship is a slow conversation of color. A rejected suitor dims its sails and folds them; an accepted one matches the rhythm until both membranes beat in the same pale cadence.

It never hunts. The only violence in its life is the storm season, when ammonia rain scours the gel and older individuals sometimes tear.
